at.step: A hash table answers equality lookup in constant time and nothing about order. Ask it for the next key larger than a given one, or for every key between two bounds, and it has no order to consult — the table itself has nothing to answer that question with.

Measured directly: a hash table's range query costs a full scan of every key it holds, because it has no order to narrow the search. A tree's range query costs only the width of the range, because the tree is already in order. That asymmetry is why such a tiny share is enough.

For the top few of a large collection, a small heap beats sorting the whole thing. Measured directly: at ten percent of the collection, the heap wins. At twenty percent, sorting everything has already won instead, because the heap bookkeeping itself grows larger as it is asked to keep more.

For membership at a scale too large to hold exactly, a Bloom filter answers in a handful of bits per key, where a wrong yes happens rarely and a wrong no never happens at all. Priced against an exact set at the identical key count, the filter is a small fraction of the size — using the bits-per-key arithmetic a different topic already verified, not re-derived here.

For grouping by an equivalence that only ever merges, union-find answers in near-constant amortised time per operation. Its one missing operation is splitting a group back apart once it has been merged — there simply is no such operation, by the structure's own design.

A trie answers a prefix query bounded only by the length of the key, not by how many keys it holds. Ask it instead for a substring buried in the middle of a word — not a prefix at all — and its own search, which only ever walks downward from the root, has no way to find it.

Confirmed directly on a constructed case: the prefix-maximum trick returns the wrong answer for a range that excludes an early, larger value, while a segment tree, built on nothing more than an associative combining rule, returns the correct one on the identical case.

at.step: The structure is chosen by the mix, not by the single biggest operation: total cost is a weighted sum over every operation, frequency times its own cost, and that ranking changes as the mix changes. The same ten million keys, the same three structures, and three different mixes each choose a different winner — and when the mix genuinely needs two things, the answer is sometimes two structures kept in sync over the identical data, the way a well known in-memory store keeps a hash table and a skip list together over one sorted collection.

items.item: The range-share crossover measured in this topic (well under one percent) is specific to the fifty-element range width, the twenty-thousand-key count and the machine used; it is a real measurement illustrating that the asymmetry is large, not a universal constant that applies at every range width or key count.

at.step: Predict: mix a small sliver of range queries into a stream that is otherwise all equality lookups. How large does that sliver have to get before a tree, kept in order the whole time, beats the hash table outright?

The trie's breaking condition (a substring query is not a prefix query) is not merely "the trie is slow at this" — the trie's own search procedure, which only ever walks from the root downward by character, has no path to a match that does not start at position zero of some stored key, so it genuinely cannot answer the question at all, not just slowly.
